title: WEEKEND READING: Points of convergence: the evolution of the UK Quality Code
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Andy Smith, Quality and Standards Manager, QAA. The key reference points underpinning quality and standards for the UK higher education sector – the Frameworks for Higher Education Qualifications, Subject Benchmarks Statements, Characteristics Statements and the Quality Code – have long since established a coherence and consistency of shared […]

The post WEEKEND READING: Points of convergence: the evolution of the UK Quality Code appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Andy Smith, Quality and Standards Manager, QAA.

The key reference points underpinning quality and standards for the UK higher education sector – the Frameworks for Higher Education Qualifications, Subject Benchmarks Statements, Characteristics Statements and the Quality Code – have long since established a coherence and consistency of shared understanding, expectations, principles and practice. Curated by the Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (QAA), these documents are crucially owned by the sector itself and co-created by colleagues across the four nations of the United Kingdom. They’ve become so central to our practices that it’s hard now to imagine how UK higher education could ever have worked – or indeed now could work – without them.

As we mark the publication of the full and comprehensive set of collections of Advice & Guidance to accompany the 2024 iteration of the UK Quality Code for Higher Education, it’s worth taking a moment to think back to the point at which their development began – a time of a very different and rather less expansive and inclusive higher education landscape – and to reflect upon the policy ambitions for participation in a consistently and reliably high-quality learning environment which this work has fundamentally supported.

Back in July 1997, Sir Ron Dearing’s National Committee of Inquiry into Higher Education (NCIHE) published some fundamental proposals for higher education in the UK. At the same time, a committee chaired by Sir Ron Garrick had examined similar changes in the Scottish higher education system. It was out of those two reports that QAA was established that year.

The Dearing report offered a vision for education promoting the development of a ‘learning society’ that would see a massive expansion of student numbers into the higher education system and focus on the ’pursuit of quality and a commitment to standards’. The report highlighted a lack of consistency in safeguarding academic standards and called for ‘greater explicitness and clarity about standards and the levels of achievement required for different awards’. The report identified the delicate balancing act required between institutional diversity and autonomy in the sector while also establishing a ‘collective responsibility’ and ‘achievement of reasonable standards of awards’.

To achieve this balance, the report recommended the creation of national qualifications frameworks. The Framework for Higher Education Qualifications (FHEQ) and the Framework for Qualifications of Higher Education Institutions in Scotland (FQHEIS) were first published by QAA in 2001.

The other major recommendation of the Dearing report was for QAA to develop a ‘code of practice which every institution should be required formally to adopt, by 2001/02, as a condition of public funding’. This code of practice later became central to an ‘Academic Infrastructure’ – an overarching system that set out the key frameworks for maintaining academic standards and for how autonomous institutions were to embed nationally agreed benchmarks and reference points into their internal mechanisms for assuring quality and enhancing the student experience.

The development of the Academic Infrastructure and its role in supporting a shared understanding of academic standards and quality was to form the foundation of the new arrangements for quality assurance and institutional audit in UK higher education post-1997.

The Further and Higher Education Act 1992 had previously required funding councils to assess the quality of education provided by institutions that received their funding – and this had been conducted through parallel processes of quality audit and assessment. These processes were later combined and consolidated by the establishment of QAA, and by its launch in 2003 of a cyclical institutional review method for English higher education institutions supported by the Academic Infrastructure to assess the reliability of standards.

Articulated through its Code of Practice, alongside the Qualifications Frameworks and Subject Benchmark Statements, the Academic Infrastructure was developed and published over a period of ten years. By 2010, QAA’s own evaluation of the Academic Infrastructure found that the Academic Infrastructure had, for the first time, brought to higher education a ‘consistent approach’ and ‘a common vocabulary about academic standards and quality’.

The original Code of Practice was not short: it ran to 175 precepts and 258 pages. It didn’t prescribe specifications for how providers were to meet its precepts, but set out how providers could assure themselves that they were making consistent decisions in the student interest and how they could work effectively to continually enhance the student experience.

QAA’s 2010 review of the Academic Infrastructure had put forward a number of proposals that would result in the development of the first iteration of the Quality Code – most notably that QAA should

‘clearly set out which components of the Academic Infrastructure are essential requirements for higher education providers when they are setting and maintaining the academic standards for which they are responsible’.

Providers were most interested in meeting those essential requirements in managing the quality of the student learning experience, as well as establishing greater clarity on how the Academic Infrastructure linked to European frameworks and how review processes related directly to the precepts.

Published in October 2010, following the formation of the Conservative-LibDem coalition government, and prior to the introduction in England of increased tuition fees, Lord Browne’s highly influential report on ‘securing a sustainable future for higher education’ had recommended the promotion of ‘genuine competition for students between institutions’ – and had advised that ‘to safeguard this approach… the HE Council enforces minimum standards of quality’.

It was during the resulting period of significant sectoral change that the various sections of the first edition of the Quality Code were published, between 2012 and 2015.

The application of the original Quality Code had varied in relation to the different review methods in place across the UK. This difference in approaches had become more pronounced by the point that the Quality Code underwent extensive revision in 2017-18, partly as a result of shifts in how the English sector was regulated, and opened up wider debates around the divergence of quality assessment and enhancement mechanisms across the four nations of the UK.

The second edition of the Quality Code was published in April 2018 and consisted of a set of four Expectations (two for ‘Standards’ and two for ‘Quality’), and a set of 17 core and common practices. What had been an overarching quality framework consisting of three parts, eleven chapters, 19 Expectations and 431 pages, had been reduced through a process of consultation and refinement to one side of A4.

While this iteration of the Code, fashioned by the exigencies of balance and compromise during a period of change and divergence, served its purpose, there was strong sector support for the development of a fuller edition of the Quality Code which would benefit from more extensive consideration of evolving contexts, challenges and approaches – and which would afford a more comprehensive and robust articulation of the convergence of the UK sector’s shared principles and effective practices.

We started work on the current edition of the Code in 2022. We published this edition – an 18-page set of 12 principles (each accompanied by a set of key practices) – in June 2024, following an extensive process of engagement, co-creation and consultation with colleagues from across the sector. The application of each of its principles has since been supported by the publication of a collection of Advice & Guidance, mapped onto its associated key practices. The first three of these were published last summer; the remaining nine have been published this month. As ever, QAA has facilitated and curated the creation of these sector-owned documents, written by experts across our sector and designed to represent both the rich diversity and the convergence of shared perspectives and effective practices which our sector encompasses – and to address the emerging challenges facing higher education today.

The Quality Code encapsulates a set of principles which remind us what matters, and what we do best, in times of change, opportunity and crisis. It acts as a common point of reference for all higher education providers, no matter their size, history or profile. It articulates our sense of value, and represents a shared resource and focus – and a common bond – through which we can work to enhance quality, secure standards and champion the student at the heart of a truly transformative educational system.

title: Comedy show row: Professor, student apologise to each other after viral video
summary: A professor from Nirma University confronted a student by the collar during a student-organized event. The incident happened after a stand-up comedy performance, where a remark was made by the student. A video of the confrontation went viral, leading to public outcry and concern. Both the professor and student have since apologized to each other after the incident.
full_text:
Professor H K Patel, the head of the department, was addressing the audience from the stage when the student made a quip from a movie.

AHMEDABAD: A day after a video of a Nirma University professor holding a student by the collar went viral, both the professor and the student have apologised to each other, sources told TOI on Friday. The university has, however, ordered a probe into the incident. It has formed a three-member high-powered committee comprising deans and directors, which will submit its report within seven days. The incident allegedly took place during ‘Technofora 2026’, a three-day event organised by students of Nirma University’s Institute of Technology from September 18 to 20. After a stand-up comedy act, Professor H K Patel, head of the department, was addressing the audience from the stage when a student made a quip from a movie, "Jaldi kar, Panvel nikalna hai," asking him to finish his speech. Sources said Prof Patel then asked the student to come on stage. A video widely shared on social media shows the professor holding the student by his collar and asking him to behave. The professor is also heard threatening the student in the video, saying, “I can go to any extent. The day you dare to insult any faculty member of the Nirma University campus, you are gone forever.” Prof R N Patel, director general of Nirma University, said the university had constituted a three-member committee to probe the incident. “Both the professor and the student have apologised to each other. However, the due process will take place. Further course of action will be decided based on the committee’s recommendations,” he said.

End of Article

title: Ireland looks overseas as minister questions international student model
summary:
Ireland's higher education minister James Lawless has urged greater focus on teaching abroad as housing and capacity pressures test further growth in Ireland’s inbound international student market.

The post Ireland looks overseas as minister questions international student model appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
James Lawless called for greater focus on delivering education overseas, warning of challenges in scaling the traditional model of bringing large numbers of international students into the country.

Lawless said there were “challenges in the traditional model of international students coming to Ireland en masse”, as he wrapped up a five-day visit to China that included trips to Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong.

“And while many bring great diversity and skills and knowledge to the system, there are pressures as that model scales in terms of resource consumption, student accommodation… visas can be problematic at times – all the things that we’re familiar with,” said Lawless, as reported by The Irish Times.

The minister said Ireland already lacked sufficient accommodation for its domestic higher education population and pointed to partnerships allowing Irish institutions to deliver qualifications overseas as another route to internationalisation.

His comments put renewed emphasis on transnational education (TNE) as Ireland continues to attract growing numbers of international students, with the latest available Higher Education Authority (HEA) data recording 44,535 non-Irish-domiciled enrolments in 2024/25, up 10.2% in a year.

India was the largest source market, accounting for 20.6% of those enrolments, followed by the US at 13.8% and China at 9.9%, while almost three-quarters of the international cohort came from outside the EU.

Lawless’s China visit offered a clear example of the overseas model, with China now Ireland’s main TNE partner and the number of joint programs between institutions in the two countries doubling since 2014.

More than 130 joint programmes involving 16 Irish higher education institutions and 54 Chinese institutions now serve over 16,000 students in China.

“This is a great testament to the positive work being undertaken by our higher education institutions,” Lawless said ahead of the trip, describing the partnerships as allowing Ireland to bring its education standards, innovation culture and academic values to China.

The minister also attended a TNE event organised by Education in Ireland and the Irish embassy in Beijing, where several Irish and Chinese higher education institutions were set to announce new partnership agreements.

The renewed emphasis on overseas delivery comes alongside Ireland’s existing international student ambitions, with the government’s Global Citizens 2030 strategy placing internationalisation at the heart of its education and research agenda.

We’re aware that there are challenges in the traditional model of international students coming to Ireland en masse

James Lawless, Ireland’s higher education minister

Speaking at The PIE Live Ireland in October 2025, Lawless described international education as “very important to Ireland”, highlighting the economic, social, cultural and academic benefits international students brought to the country.

“For international students, our aspiration is simple: that each one experiences a genuine Irish welcome,” he said at the time, while also acknowledging accommodation as a key challenge.

The tension between international growth and domestic capacity predates those comments, with government official Ian McKenna telling The PIE in 2024 that attracting international students onto Irish campuses was “absolutely critical” while acknowledging pressures around housing and visas.

Those pressures now extend beyond accommodation, with universities warning that rising enrolments and costs are stretching a higher education system struggling to keep pace with demand.

As The PIE News reported this week, the chairs of six universities backed calls for €190 million in additional annual core funding, warning that the sector faces an annual shortfall of more than €250m despite increased state support.

The seven universities represented by the Irish Universities Association (IUA) enrolled more than 10,000 additional students between 2022 and 2024, a 7% increase without a corresponding rise in funding, according to the chairs.

Across the wider system, enrolments reached 278,880 in 2024/25, rising 4.9% in a year and marking the largest annual percentage increase since 2020/21.

Against that backdrop, Lawless’s latest intervention points to a broader model of internationalisation in which Ireland continues to host international students while its institutions expand their reach through education delivered abroad.

“This allows us to bring our education standards, our innovation culture and academic values to China,” Lawless said of the partnerships.

title: ‘A massive punch in the face’: Students pay the price for ILAC’s sudden collapse
summary:
Current and incoming ILAC students and their families tell The PIE of tuition at risk, cancelled travel and immigration uncertainty, as language learners receive replacement classes while career-college students await answers.

The post ‘A massive punch in the face’: Students pay the price for ILAC’s sudden collapse appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
For José Carlos Chávez, two years of plans in Vancouver began to unravel before he boarded the plane.

The Guadalajara photographer was due to start a Sales and Marketing diploma at ILAC International College in mid-October, after paying nearly CAD$14,000, securing an apartment and receiving study permit approval.

Instead, Chávez cancelled his journey and began trying to recover money committed to an education that would no longer be delivered.

“ILAC as an institution has still provided zero direct communication or official closure notification to my email,” he told The PIE News.

Chávez contacted KPMG, trustee for ILAC, and submitted proof of payment. He said the firm was assessing the company’s assets but did not currently expect a distribution to unsecured creditors.

His landlord waived the roughly CAD$1,800 lease-cancellation penalty, but Flair Airlines provided only around 30% of his flight costs as travel credit.

His travel is now on hold while he searches for another institution and navigates the requirements for changing his designated learning institution.

Private colleges have advertised “rescue packages”, but Chávez said those he found required fresh tuition after students had already lost money to the group.

ILAC Education Group included the language school International Language Academy of Canada and the career-focused ILAC International College.

Both ceased operations on September 18 and cancelled their programs with immediate effect. KPMG’s bankruptcy proceeding, however, specifically names International Language Academy of Canada Inc. as the bankrupt entity.

ILAC blamed mounting financial pressures over the previous three years and “significant regulatory changes affecting the sector”, saying it lacked the resources to continue operating.

The group promised direct information about programs, student services and next steps. However, every student and parent who spoke to The PIE said neither ILAC International College nor the wider group contacted them individually.

An outdated automated reply from an ILAC address was still telling correspondents that it was closed for an October public holiday and classes would resume the following day.

In Vancouver, Sebastián Cáceres discovered the news when a friend sent him ILAC’s Instagram post minutes after it appeared.

The Chilean-Bolivian student initially suspected the account had been hacked, before a former teacher confirmed the closure and said staff had learned during a Zoom meeting shortly before the announcement.

Cáceres had studied Sales and Marketing at ILAC International College’s Vancouver campus for around a year and expected to finish next March, having paid almost CAD$13,000.

“All the information that we got was for ourselves,” he said, describing students searching social media and approaching lawyers, teachers and even ChatGPT because calls and emails went unanswered.

The uncertainty has disrupted Cáceres’s job search, as he believes his work authorisation is affected and is awaiting clarity on whether he needs new documentation.

With accommodation alone costing at least CAD$1,500 a month, he fears that even one to three weeks without work could cause serious hardship.

“It’s like a huge, massive punch in the face,” he said, calling for urgent immigration guidance and additional time on students’ permits.

The fallout stretches beyond students already in Canada.

Clayton Jorge enrolled his son, Daniel, in ILAC International College’s Toronto-based Business Certificate: Introduction to Project Management course a month before the closure, for July 2027.

The family booked through a Brazilian education agency that had worked with ILAC for years, but Jorge said neither they nor the agency received any warning.

“We have never had any direct communication with ILAC, either before or after the incident,” he said, adding that even the agency was “caught completely by surprise”.

The agency is seeking a transfer, but a comparable July course may be unavailable during Brazil’s school holidays, potentially forcing the family to consider another city or country.

It’s not just for us, it’s for everybody. The teachers were doing their jobs all week, and in five minutes they lost everything

Sebastián Cáceres

Comments beneath ILAC’s social media announcements painted a picture of students already en route to Canada, families awaiting refunds and accommodation providers that had not received full payment.

Agents and former employees have also said they received no warning, with some alleging that the group accepted new enrolments shortly before it ceased operating.

Cáceres said the consequences extended beyond students: “It’s not just for us, it’s for everybody. The teachers were doing their jobs all week, and in five minutes they lost everything.”

The support available now depends on which ILAC institution and program a student attended.

Languages Canada said on September 22 that it had placed more than 430 of the 1,362 current in-person students displaced from ILAC’s language programs at other member schools, prioritising those finishing soonest.

Its Education Completion Assurance Plan provides comparable replacement language courses without additional tuition, but is not a refund or insurance scheme and excludes travel, accommodation, insurance and learning materials.

The organisation also contacted online language students and aimed to begin placing them in similar accredited programs by September 28.

However, the plan excludes ILAC International College’s career and co-op programs, leaving students such as Chávez and Cáceres dependent on provincial protection systems and government decisions.

British Columbia’s Private Training Institutions Regulatory Unit (PTIRU) said four ILAC Education Group institutions — ILAC, ILAC International College, Tamwood Careers and Tamwood Language Centres — surrendered their designation certificates on September 18.

ILAC acquired Tamwood in 2023. The regulator said eligible students in approved programs may claim against the province’s Student Tuition Protection Fund.

Ontario’s Training Completion Assurance Fund can generally provide eligible career-college students with training completion or a refund, but, as of September 24, no ILAC-specific guidance on eligibility, timelines or arrangements for incoming and co-op students had been published.

The group closed four days after EC English ceased teaching across 25 schools in seven countries. Languages Canada said all 471 students at EC’s Canadian locations were placed elsewhere within four days, but described ILAC as a more complex challenge.

The PIE contacted ILAC, KPMG and regulators in British Columbia and Ontario; KPMG sent an automated acknowledgement, while no substantive responses had been received by publication.

For Chávez, any solution must prevent students who paid ILAC International College from having to fund a second course elsewhere.

“At this stage my primary goal is seeking a clear, fair path from Canadian authorities that recognises affected students without forcing us to pay twice for an institutional bankruptcy we had no control over,” he said.

title: How Pakistan’s education agents can evolve with the international student market
summary:
As international education demand continues to grow in Pakistan, the next challenge is not simply recruiting more students. It is building a market that students, families and institutions can trust.

The post How Pakistan’s education agents can evolve with the international student market appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Pakistan is a market with strong demand for international education, and education agents play an important role in helping students navigate what can be a complicated process. For many students and families, the decision involves far more than choosing a university. It can mean significant financial commitments, language testing, visa requirements and, in many cases, a major decision for the whole family.

That makes the quality of advice students receive particularly important.

There are established agents in Pakistan that have spent years building institutional relationships, developing market knowledge and earning the trust of students and families. At the same time, the growth of international education has brought new agencies and counsellors into the market. The result is a landscape where experience, capability and professional standards can vary considerably.

That should not lead to a conversation about whether agents are good or bad. The more useful question is how the market can become more professional as it grows.

Compliance has to become integral to the job

Being able to process an application is no longer enough. Students need advisers who understand the differences between institutions, courses and destinations, who can explain the implications of their choices and who are willing to tell a student when an option may not be right for them.

That last point matters. A good counsellor should sometimes be prepared to say, “I don’t think this is the right university for you.” That is harder to do when the focus is primarily on the transaction.

Compliance should be seen as the minimum standard, not the definition of quality

Compliance should therefore not be treated as something that sits in a back office or is revisited when an institution asks for an audit. It needs to be part of everyday counselling and decision-making.

That means investing in staff training, keeping up with changes in immigration and institutional requirements, being transparent about institutional relationships and responsibilities, and knowing when a question needs to be referred to someone with the appropriate expertise.

But compliance should be seen as the minimum standard, not the definition of quality. The better agents will be those that build trust through the quality of their advice, not simply the number of applications they submit.

Credibility also means transparency

For students and families, credibility should be relatively easy to test. If an agent says it represents a particular university, students should be able to verify that relationship. Institutions, in turn, should make their authorised representatives reasonably easy for students to identify and verify.

Agents in Pakistan are often proud to display their British Council training credentials, and rightly so. The training provides useful knowledge and awareness of the UK as a study destination. But it is worth noting that the British Council itself does not formally endorse, accredit or validate agents or counsellors through its training programme. The certificate and badge demonstrate an individual’s training and knowledge; they are not an accreditation of the agency or a guarantee of the quality of its service.

Less often discussed is the fact that the British Council’s own guide to choosing an education agent advises students to ask whether an agent is paid a commission by the schools, colleges or universities they promote. The guide notes that such arrangements are common, but makes an important distinction: regardless of whether an agent receives commission, students should receive high-quality and unbiased advice.

That is an important principle for any market. Transparency about institutional relationships and commercial arrangements does not undermine the role of agents. It strengthens it. Students and families should have enough information to understand the advice they are receiving and make an informed decision about what is right for them.

A professional market should not depend on students simply taking an agent’s word for it.

Institutions have a role in the market they help create

It is also too easy to make this solely an agent story. Universities and other institutions have responsibilities too. Institutions rightly need to manage recruitment risk and protect academic and immigration compliance. They also need to be increasingly careful about who represents them in a market. But the relationship cannot simply be: institution sets the target, agent delivers the applications. The incentives institutions create matter.

If volume is consistently prioritised over student fit, if agents receive inconsistent information, if too many partners are appointed without meaningful oversight, or if major recruitment decisions are communicated with little warning, institutions can contribute to the very problems they are trying to manage.

Good agent management therefore has to be more than maintaining a list of approved representatives. It means selecting partners carefully, training them properly, communicating changes clearly and evaluating the quality of the students and applications they bring. The responsibility for recruitment quality cannot be completely outsourced to the agent.

Agents are often the first to see what is changing

There is another reason institutions should engage seriously with good agents: they are often close to the student long before an institution is.

An agent may hear the same concern from dozens of students before it becomes visible in an institution’s data. They hear the questions parents are asking, see where misinformation is spreading and understand which parts of an application or visa process are creating confusion.

That does not mean every piece of feedback from an agent should be accepted uncritically. It does mean that this information has value.

Pakistan is also not a single recruitment market. Student behaviour and access to international education can differ significantly between major cities and smaller centres, while family influence and word of mouth can play an important role in how students make decisions. A university trying to understand the market from a distance will see only part of the picture.

The strongest institutions will use their relationships with credible agents not simply to generate applications, but also to understand what is happening on the ground.

When policy changes, students carry the consequences

This becomes particularly important when institutions or destinations change their approach to a market.

There are legitimate reasons for institutions to tighten recruitment, change entry requirements or reconsider their exposure to particular markets. Risk cannot simply be ignored because agents or students have already invested in a recruitment cycle. But the way those decisions are communicated matters.

An agent may already be working with a student who has spent months preparing, paid for tests and applications, made financial plans and persuaded their family that a particular route is achievable. When an institution changes its position suddenly, the agent is often left explaining the consequences. Ultimately, it is the student who has the most to lose.

Better communication between institutions, agents and the wider sector cannot eliminate recruitment risk. It can, however, reduce the chance that students are caught between decisions made at different points in the recruitment chain.

The next phase should be about confidence, not just volume

Pakistan does not necessarily need fewer education agents. It needs a market in which students and institutions can more easily distinguish between those providing professional advice and those simply processing applications.

Established agents have a responsibility to raise standards and share good practice. Newer agencies entering the market need to understand that sustainable growth will require more than opening an office, signing institutional agreements and generating applications.

The individual counsellor matters just as much as the agency’s brand. Training, knowledge, professional development and accountability need to become part of the conversation about agent quality.

Institutions have a responsibility to be more selective about their partners and more serious about how they manage those relationships.

And the wider sector has a role in creating clearer expectations around what good recruitment looks like.

The real measure of a mature agent market is not simply how many students it sends overseas. It is whether students are making informed decisions, whether institutions have confidence in the recruitment they receive, and whether problems are identified early enough to be addressed.

Pakistan has the demand and the ambition to remain an important international education market.

The next step is making sure that growth is matched by the professional standards needed to sustain it. A bigger agent market is not necessarily a better one. A more trusted one would be.

title: ‘So, where do I fit in?’: Making a university’s learning and teaching strategy relevant to professional services staff
summary: The post ‘So, where do I fit in?’: Making a university’s learning and teaching strategy relevant to professional services staff appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Heather Walker, Laura Montgomerie and Emeritus Professor Bethan Wood, University of Glasgow consider how a university Learning and Teaching Strategy was made relevant to the work of professional services staff.

A conundrum was identified in the School of Social and Environmental Sustainability, University of Glasgow, when the authors pondered: how can we make the University Strategies relevant to the work of the School’s Professional Services Staff?

The background

“So, where do I fit in?” It’s a question that surfaced repeatedly during personal development reviews with our team of nine professional services staff. Based on a rural campus with a broad remit, we wear many hats – programme support, timetabling, quality assurance, student experience, finance, and more. Yet despite being deeply embedded in the day-to-day life of the University, there was a shared uncertainty about how our work connected to the institution’s learning and teaching strategy.

The review conversations revealed a common theme: colleagues struggled to see how their roles contributed to the bigger strategic picture. The University’s strategy spoke confidently about academic excellence, student experience, and teaching quality – but where did professional services sit within that narrative?

Faced with this challenge, the team reflected on the best approach to ensure that academic colleagues could appreciate professional services’ valuable contribution to the delivery of the University strategy at all levels. It was agreed that an in-person, interactive workshop involving all parties would be the best way forward.

We wanted to frame this challenge within a conceptual model that could make our contribution visible and tangible and identified Porter’s Value Chain as a helpful lens. Although traditionally used in business contexts, it provided a practical way to map how value is created across the institution.

Together, we reframed learning and teaching as the University’s “primary activity,” with professional services—including our own work—as essential support activities that enable excellence. Seeing our work visualised in this way was incredibly affirming. It demonstrated how administrative efficiency directly shapes teaching quality, student wellbeing, and academic integrity.

The workshop

After some research, the team thought that the University’s Learning and Teaching Strategy (2021-25; University of Glasgow, 2025a) would be suitable for a workshop, considering that most of the Professional Services (PS) staff had roles as programme administrators. Luckily, the University had published this Strategy on a single page (University of Glasgow, 2025b) and this could utilised in the workshop as a template for annotating where PS staff had input into the Strategy in their daily work.

Most of the School’s PS staff attended the workshop since it fell on a day and time when they would normally have a PS staff meeting – this is important because the workload of each is high (covering many roles) and even taking an hour or two out of their week means that they then have to catch-up on their normal work. The workshop was introduced by Bethan as hopefully demonstrating to them how the work they undertake is relevant to University Strategy. Each was given a hard copy of the Strategy on a page and Bethan ran through the components of the strategy, i.e., Purpose, Values, Pillars (and Enablers) and Outcomes. Then, using her experience as an academic, she showed how some components were relevant to the work of the School’s academics. Following this, Bethan than chose some content to demonstrate how they were relevant to the work of some of the PS staff in the workshop e.g., the support provided by the programme and course administrators to convening academic staff and the students who are undertaking placements.

Each PS staff then annotated their hard copy of the Strategy on a page and when completed, fed back on some of the work they had identified as relevant to the Strategy. The workshop concluded with staff reflecting on what they had learnt from the workshop.

The reflection

The workshop emphasised how our operational tasks contribute to our strategic goals. It became clear that our policies, procedures, and administrative functions have a broader impact than we initially realised. The importance of accuracy in our roles was highlighted, as the tasks performed by professional services often underpin the overall strategy. By ensuring our procedures are streamlined and effective, and our service delivery is efficient, we can positively influence our strategic outcomes.

Additionally, the workshop fostered a culture of partnership between our academic colleagues and us. It revealed that their engagement and understanding of our processes and procedures are essential, as they directly contribute to them. If they become more involved with us and share our commitment to accuracy and quality, even small improvements can yield significant benefits over time, enhancing our operations and aligning with our strategic objectives.

When tasks within the professional services team require input from academics, it is crucial that they engage appropriately. This collaboration enables us to complete tasks swiftly and accurately, thereby minimising the time academics spend away from their work. If the infrastructure is stable and efficient, it benefits the whole school. By reducing administrative errors, we can improve the student experience, lessen student stress, and help academics manage their workload more effectively.

The workshop helped us identify additional opportunities for collaboration with our academic partners. We can now clearly articulate how our joint efforts impact the overall strategy, ensuring that we are all working towards the same goals.

Final thoughts

Potentially any university strategy can be made appropriate to the work of its staff. By taking elements of the strategy and providing some examples of where there is relevance, we can assist staff in making further connections themselves. If successful, then staff will feel more empowered in their day-to-day activities, because they will recognise, and understand, why they have been asked to undertake this work.

References

Porter, M.E., 1985. Competitive Advantage: Creating and Sustaining Superior Performance. The Free Press.

University of Glasgow, 2025a. About Learning and Teaching Strategy. [Online). Available at: https://www.gla.ac.uk/myglasgow/learningandteaching/about/ . [Accessed 17th September 2025]

University of Glasgow, 2025b. Learning and Teaching Strategy on a page. [Online). Available at: https://www.gla.ac.uk/media/Media_842672_smxx.pdf . [Accessed 17th September 2025]

Heather is a Programme Administrator in the Student and Academic Operations team at the School of Social and Environmental Sustainability, University of Glasgow. She has responsibility for the Education degree portfolio and coordinates the operational aspects of school placements. Heather also supports whole-school student-advising processes, as well as managing interviews for teaching degrees.

Laura is the Student Experience and Operations Manager in the School of Social and Environmental Sustainability, University of Glasgow. She has worked in the Higher Education sector for almost 2 decades, at several sector leading institutions in both academic and professional service roles. Her experience has been focused in the areas of Learning and Teaching, Academic Policy & Quality Assurance and more recently, Student Experience.

Bethan is formerly a Professor of Ecology and Deputy Head of School (Staff and Student Experience) in the School of Social and Environmental Sustainability, University of Glasgow. She is a Fellow of the Royal Society of Biology and a Chartered Biologist. She is also a Principal Fellow of the Higher Education Academy and a Fellow of the Linnean Society.

title: When Student Care Becomes Unsustainable for Faculty
summary: Chavella T. Pittman, Dominican University   I'm overwhelmed with teaching/mentoring students. . . . And the university doesn't value my . . . labor devoted to supporting students."—Woman faculty of color at a research university Faculty care.  We care about students’ learning, their well-being, their development, their futures. We care enough to redesign assignments, rewrite policies, overhaul entire courses, and re-imagine whole semesters when circumstances demand it. I’ve spent decades...
full_text:
Chavella T. Pittman, Dominican University

I'm overwhelmed with teaching/mentoring students. . . . And the university doesn't value my . . . labor devoted to supporting students."—Woman faculty of color at a research university

Faculty care. We care about students’ learning, their well-being, their development, their futures. We care enough to redesign assignments, rewrite policies, overhaul entire courses, and re-imagine whole semesters when circumstances demand it. I’ve spent decades helping faculty implement effective yet efficient teaching practices in support of their success and well-being.

But in recent years, something has shifted. Increasingly, the institutional expectation is not only that faculty care, but that we should provide student care endlessly—expansively, exhaustively, and without limits.

In my work with faculty and campuses nationwide, I’ve noticed that the meaning of “good teaching” has quietly started to drift. It’s shifted towards a model in which faculty perform significant amounts of student care—addressing students’ personal, emotional, logistical, and sometimes crisis-related needs, in addition to pedagogical care.

Emerging research suggests that the more faculty take on student care responsibilities( no matter how much they truly desire to help), their burnout increases, and this has negative outcomes for faculty well-being as well as student success (Eisenberg et al., 2024).

What Counts as “Student Care”?

Faculty often describe student care as:

Responding to personal crises

Helping students navigate bureaucratic or logistical barriers

Providing emotional reassurance

Extending flexibility far beyond course design

Adopting roles of social worker, therapist, crisis counselor, or parent

Offering individualized support unrelated to learning conditions

In other words, student care attends primarily to needs outside the instructional sphere. It is responsive, relational, and deeply humane. But it is also boundless—because students’ needs are boundless. When institutions position student care as a hallmark of “good teaching,” they implicitly transfer responsibility for student support systems onto individual faculty, who cannot possibly meet these needs at scale or alone.

Pedagogical Care Is A Different Form of Care Entirely

Pedagogical care, by contrast, is the care we extend through teaching:

Designing clear, transparent assignments

Building predictable structures that also include flexibility

Creating meaningful opportunities for practice and feedback

Using inclusive teaching methods that support varied learners

Setting boundaries that foster autonomy & model well-being

Providing opportunities for connection without becoming the connection itself

Pedagogical care is bounded by instructional purpose. It isn’t about solving students’ external problems—it’s about designing and facilitating learning in ways that acknowledge students’ humanity while still centering the academic mission.

When we do not differentiate between these two forms of care, faculty often feel a pervasive pressure to “do everything” in their teaching. And it means institutions erroneously interpret pedagogical care primarily through the lens of personal service to individual students rather than through the accurate lens of systemic design for learning.

Understanding Faculty Care: Three Forms of Labor

Conversations about faculty care labor are often reduced to “emotional labor,” which individualizes both the work and the burnout. But teaching—especially when entangled with student care—requires at least three forms of labor. I discuss these more fully in my book Empowered (Pittman, 2025), but in short here’s what they are and how they might show up in faculty’s teaching labor (and overwhelm or burnout):

Emotional labor is producing, modifying, or repressing your own emotions while teaching. In pedagogical care it shows up as staying patient, encouraging, approachable. In student care it looks like absorbing students’ distress, frustration, or crisis.

Affective labor involves managing students’ emotions and relationship dynamics in the classroom. As pedagogical care it comprises building trust, creating belonging, or fostering engagement. As student care it involves maintaining endless availability, constant reassurance, or enmeshed personal connection.

Cognitive labor refers to the thinking, planning, strategizing, and problem-solving required to get and keep teaching up and running. As pedagogical care it encompasses designing assignments, curating content, or creating structure. As student care it entails a ceaseless tracking of each student’s circumstances, exceptions, and needs.

When student care is normalized as good teaching, faculty perform all three forms of the above labor at intensities that exceed what any one person can sustainably provide.

The problem isn’t that faculty are unwilling to care. The problem is that student care has become a structural expectation for teaching masquerading as individual faculty virtue.

The Institutional Drift Toward Boundless Care

Over the last decade, many campuses have experienced a rapid expansion of what “good teaching” is assumed to include (Mowreader, 2024).Syllabi are increasingly expected to be comprehensive wellness documents. Faculty policies are scrutinized through a “customer service” lens. Students often seek immediate, individualized support from faculty for challenges that used to be navigated through institutional offices.

At the same time, the landscape students inhabit truly has changed—financial instability, political climate, caregiving responsibilities, and competing demands are real. But rather than investing in robust, accessible institutional supports, many campuses rely on faculty to absorb these pressures directly via their teaching.

This drift isn’t always stated outright. Instead, it shows up subtly when administrators or teaching center staff say to faculty:

“Faculty who care about students/student success would…”

“Students need a place to process…”

“Faculty should anticipate that students need …”

“To protect students’ fragile mental health you should…”

“Students need you to understand…”

“Faculty who are committed to [insert current institutionally valued principle] would…”

Even well-intentioned teaching literature often collapses student care and pedagogical care into one category of “student support,” blurring the boundaries and magnifying expectations of faculty labor.

When every student problem is framed as a problem faculty must personally solve, teaching becomes structurally unsustainable.

A Path Forward: Redefining “Good Teaching”

A sustainable and effective model of teaching would treat pedagogical care as required, as it is fundamental to our teaching role and student learning. It would also treat student care as optional and bounded. That is, faculty can choose to engage in student care—and many of us will—but it must not be the default definition of good teaching. And this model would include institutional student care as essential because good teaching requires campus systems that must meet the student needs that faculty cannot and should not meet individually. In other words, we must shift the question from, “How can faculty care more?” to “What forms of care most effectively support learning and belong within the faculty teaching role?”

Name the conflation explicitly.

The scholarship of teaching and learning, administrators, and faculty should clearly differentiate student care from pedagogical care rather than treat all student support practices as interchangeable.

Protect and reward pedagogical care as instructional work.

Faculty should be supported, evaluated, and rewarded in review procedures for their often invisible pedagogical care that improves student learning and not shamed for not investing inordinate labor into unacknowledged student care.

Re/build institutional student support systems.

Good teaching is dependent upon institutional investment in student care. When institutions frame faculty as the primary responders to student needs, they absolve themselves of the responsibility to create robust, accessible, well-resourced support infrastructures.

Closing Thoughts

It boils down to this: Faculty should reduce their student care labor and reinvest in pedagogical care.Not because students don’t deserve support, but because student care is a structural need that requires structural solutions and pedagogical care produces learning. Good teaching is not boundless student care labor. In fact, that type of teaching leads to faculty burnout and overwhelm with negative outcomes for both faculty and students. Instead, good teaching is bounded, intentional, pedagogically grounded care that supports learning, respects faculty labor, and is embedded in a university ecosystem capable of meeting student needs holistically.

References

Mowreader, A. (2024, January 30). Student wellness tip: Helping faculty help students. Inside Higher Ed. Inside Higher Ed.

Pittman, C. T. (2025). Empowered: A Woman faculty of Color's guide to teaching and thriving. University of Oklahoma Press.

title: Political psychology: Why extremist parties are thriving and what democratic politicians can do against it
summary: Far-right and far-left parties are celebrating success after success, leaving moderate politicians in the dust and worrying many Germans. Political psychology helps us understand what's behind growing polarization.
full_text:
On September 6, Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt held elections for its state parliament. The big winner: The right-wing AfD (Alternative for Germany) party, which garnered 43.8% of the votes; more than ever before.

It's still unclear who will govern the state because the AfD does not have an absolute majority.

But it was a landslide win for the AfD, whose Saxony-Anhalt branch is classified as right-wing extremist by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, and that worries many Germans.

The day after the election, Chancellor Friedrich Merz from the conservative CDU said he was "deeply shocked" by the election results. "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany."

Merz's CDU lost more than half its share of the ballot compared to the last state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The CDU dropped from 37.1% in 2021 to 17.2% in 2026.

Two weeks later, at state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on September 20, the CDU didn't even make the 5% threshold to enter parliament.

It was the first time ever for the CDU; they got only 4.9% of the vote in the northeastern state. The strongest party was once again the AfD with 38.2%.

That same day, in the city state of Berlin, the socialist Left Party won the election and will likely govern Germany's capital. In Berlin, the CDU was the second-strongest party and the AfD came in third.

Germans worried about rise of far-right, far-left parties

These state elections show that parties on the extreme ends of the political spectrum are growing stronger in Germany.

The country has experience with both extreme right- and left-wing governments: the Nazis that led Germany into World War II and the Socialist Unity Party (SED) that ruled then-East Germany from 1949 until 1989.

A return to extreme politics is a scary proposition for some people.

In a representative monthly survey called "What worries the world?", the polling institute Ipsos found that almost one-fifth of Germans (18%) said they were worried by growing extremism in the country when they asked about 1,000 people between the ages of 16 and 74 years in March and April 2026.

Generally, people in Germany are concerned about where their country is going. In the Ipsos survey, 82% said they saw Germany as moving in the wrong direction.

How to measure a country's mood

Asking people about their fears or worries is just one way to take the nation's temperature. There are other options to measure politically relevant emotions in the population as well.

Kerstin Pahl, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin, told DW that possibilities include quantitative and qualitative surveys, as well as analyzing online discourse and the content people share on social media. It's also possible to read a nation's sentiment by observing real-life displays of emotions, like public protests and demonstrations.

For researchers like Pahl, it's also interesting to see how political issues can come to symbolize much more than their material or factual meaning.

"People may see their region's ailing infrastructure not just as proof of a lack of investment, but also as a sign that they have been forgotten [by their leaders]," said Pahl.

Affective polarization: Political opponents become the enemy

Extremist parties winning a higher percentage of the votes is what we see on the surface. Below that lie two kinds of societal polarization: Affective and ideological polarization.

"Affective polarization is a growing hatred for the political opponent. Most studies investigated this in the context of the US between supporters of the Democrat and the Republican Party," Eva Walther, head of the social psychology department at the University of Trier in western Germany, told DW. "When this happens on the party level, it's a problem."

Politicians of different parties often have to work together and reach compromises. They don't need to like each other, but they should treat each other with respect, Walther said.

"When this respectful attitude starts crumbling, it's a problem for democracy," she added.

Ideological polarization: Which problem is the most pressing?

The other phenomenon, ideological polarization, is when society is split into distinct groups based on what issues people view as the most pressing problem for them.

For example, many people to the right of the political center in Germany see migration as the biggest problem, while many people to the left of the political center say it's the climate crisis.

When different crisis situations occur at the same time, such as migration and climate change, researchers refer to a "polycrisis."

Polycrises intensify ideological polarization, making it even harder for societies to find a common way forward.

"At the moment, we have the climate crisis overlapping with an affordable energy crisis, more of an economic problem," Walther said.

In the eyes of those for whom the climate crisis is the most urgent issue, fossil fuels should be abandoned as soon as possible. But for those most concerned with affordable energy, relying only on renewable energy sources would needlessly raise prices.

People want politicians to take their problems seriously

The belief that a politician is competent and willing to tackle major challenges, to act, is a big factor in how much people trust democracy.

But that's also what makes overlapping crises so hard to manage: No matter which problems politicians attempt to solve first, one part of the population will be disappointed.

"Polycrises make it difficult for politicians to act, which means that people have less trust that politicians can solve the problems important to them," Walther said.

Right-wing extremist parties, however, aim to "satisfy people by giving them simplified answers to complex problems," added Walther.

This leads people to believe that extremist politicians can solve their problems ― which in turn leads to growing polarization.

But politicians from democratic parties can learn from clinical research to tackle this dilemma, according to Walther.

"When a person is in pain and goes to see a doctor, it's important that the doctor recognizes the patient's pain," she said.

Even if the doctor can't instantly solve the issue and make the pain go away, showing that they take the issue and the patient seriously is crucial. And the same goes for politicians.

"They need to make people's needs the first priority in their daily work," Walther said. "People want to be seen, so it's important for politicians to make it clear that they see and understand their problems."

Whether it's a doctor failing a patient or politicians failing the electorate, patient and electorate are likely to scream — and that's a signal we can all read.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

title: EUA für den Aufbau der „European University Leadership Academy“ ausgewählt
summary: Die European University Association (EUA) wurde ausgewählt, um im Rahmen des Programms Erasmus+ Fördermittel für den Aufbau einer umfassenden „European University Leadership...
full_text:
Die European University Association (EUA) wurde ausgewählt, um im Rahmen des Programms Erasmus+ Fördermittel für den Aufbau einer umfassenden „European University Leadership Academy“ zu erhalten.

Aufbauend auf den Erfahrungen des Leadership Development Programme der EUA wird die neue Akademie einen breiter angelegten europäischen Rahmen für die Führungskräfteentwicklung an Hochschulen schaffen und die Möglichkeiten für derzeitige und angehende Führungskräfte an Hochschulen in ganz Europa erweitern.

Während einer 24-monatigen Pilotphase wird die EUA das Projekt gemeinsam mit dem CHE Centrum für Hochschulentwicklung in Deutschland und der Universität für Weiterbildung Krems in Österreich als assoziierten Partnern sowie der European Association for the Applied Sciences in Higher Education (EURASHE) als assoziiertem Partner leiten.

Die Akademie wird ein skalierbares europäisches System zur Führungskräfteentwicklung entwickeln und erproben, das folgende Elemente kombiniert:

innovative Schulungsformate;

angewandte Forschung und Wissensgenerierung; sowie

Austausch unter Gleichgesinnten und Gemeinschaftsbildung.

Darüber hinaus wird sie vier sich ergänzende Formate erproben:

Module zur Führungskräfteentwicklung, die sich mit zentralen Herausforderungen im Hochschulwesen befassen;

Foresight-Labore mit den Schwerpunkten Resilienz und Nachhaltigkeit;

ein europäisches Mentoring-Programm zur Unterstützung weiblicher Führungskräfte im Hochschulbereich;

Praxisgemeinschaften, die institutionenübergreifendes Lernen ermöglichen.

Parallel dazu wird ein „Knowledge Hub“ frei zugängliche Ressourcen sowie kuratierte Erkenntnisse aus Politik und Forschung bereitstellen, während ein europäischer Gipfel für Führungskräfte im Hochschulwesen (European Higher Education Leadership Summit) und ein Alumni-Netzwerk den langfristigen Aufbau einer Gemeinschaft und den Dialog fördern sollen.

Als erstes integriertes Ökosystem zur Führungskräfteentwicklung auf europäischer Ebene dieser Art wird die Akademie vor dem Hintergrund eines sich beschleunigenden Wandels dem wachsenden Bedarf an strukturierter, länderübergreifender Führungskräfteentwicklung gerecht werden. Durch die Zusammenführung von Ausbildung, Forschung, Politik und Praxis wird die Akademie ein nachhaltiges und übertragbares Modell für die Führungskräfteentwicklung etablieren, institutionelle Kapazitäten stärken und den Wandel im gesamten europäischen Hochschulraum unterstützen.

Die Umsetzung des Projekts wird voraussichtlich Ende 2026 beginnen.

title: AI a scuola, il modello del semaforo che guida studenti e docenti
summary:
La Cheshire Academy affida a un modello a semaforo le regole per l’IA nelle attività didattiche: rosso, giallo e verde indicano quando usarla. L’obiettivo è spostare la scuola dal controllo dei compiti all’AI literacy, formando studenti capaci di verificare output, fonti ed errori

L'articolo AI a scuola, il modello del semaforo che guida studenti e docenti proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
Il problema non è più stabilire se gli studenti useranno l’intelligenza artificiale, ma insegnare loro quando, come e perché utilizzarla. L’esperienza di una scuola americana introduce un modello semplice, quello del “semaforo”, e propone un cambio di paradigma: dall’AI detection all‘AI literacy.

L’arrivo dell’intelligenza artificiale generativa nelle scuole a livello mondiale ha prodotto, in pochi anni, una trasformazione che ha colto molti sistemi educativi impreparati. ChatGPT, per primo, e gli altri chatbot sono entrati non solo metaforicamente nelle tasche degli studenti attraverso gli smartphone, rendendo possibile ottenere in pochi secondi una spiegazione, un riassunto, una traduzione, un testo argomentativo o la soluzione di un esercizio.

La prima reazione della scuola – e quella del sistema educativo italiano non è stata da meno – è stata spesso quella del controllo: vietare, limitare, individuare l’uso dell’IA nei compiti, cercare strumenti capaci di riconoscere un testo generato artificialmente.

Questa strategia presenta un limite evidente: l’IA generativa è ormai parte dell’ambiente digitale nel quale gli studenti vivono e studiano. Pensare infatti di poterla semplicemente espellere dalla scuola rischia di produrre una contraddizione: vietarla nell’apprendimento significa lasciare che siano altri contesti, spesso privi di una guida educativa, a insegnare ai ragazzi come utilizzarla.

La questione diventa allora un’altra e sono in molti nel settore dell’istruzione a porsi la domanda, ovvero non come impedire l’uso dell’IA, piuttosto come educare a un suo uso intelligente.

La Cheshire Academy e l’educazione all’uso dell’IA a scuola

Un interessante caso di studio arriva proprio dalla Cheshire Academy, scuola privata statunitense del Connecticut che accoglie circa 400 studenti dalla nona alla dodicesima classe[1].

L’esperienza è stata descritta da MIT Technology Review The Kids issue | MIT Technology Review e mostra un approccio particolarmente interessante perché non parte dalla scelta di uno specifico strumento tecnologico. La scuola non impone né vieta agli insegnanti di utilizzare l’IA, e non prescrive un’unica piattaforma: chatbot generalisti come ChatGPT e Perplexity convivono con applicazioni pensate specificamente per la scuola, come MagicSchool. La formazione dei docenti si è concentrata sulle tecniche generali di utilizzo dell’IA — compreso il prompting — ma anche sui suoi limiti: errori, informazioni inventate, bias, problemi di affidabilità.

Il punto centrale, che vedremo emerge da questa esperienza nella scuola nordamericana, non è quindi quale tecnologia utilizzare, ma quali competenze sviluppare per utilizzarla. La formazione dei docenti si è spesso concentrata sulle tecniche generali di utilizzo dell’IA, compreso il prompting, sui suoi limiti, errori, informazioni inventate, bias e problemi di affidabilità.

Conoscere un elenco di applicazioni conta meno che sviluppare una competenza trasferibile: sapere cosa chiedere all’IA, valutare ciò che restituisce, decidere se e come utilizzarlo. È una distinzione utile anche per la formazione dei docenti italiani.

Il modello del semaforo per l’IA nelle attività scolastiche

Uno degli strumenti più semplici sperimentati dalla Cheshire Academy è anche uno dei più interessanti dal punto di vista didattico è il traffic light model, il modello del semaforo, che come vedremo può essere facilmente esportabile come buona pratica.

Rosso, giallo e verde: le regole del modello

Le attività scolastiche vengono contrassegnate con tre colori.

Rosso: l’uso dell’IA non è consentito.

Giallo: l’uso dell’IA è consentito solo per alcune funzioni o attraverso determinati strumenti.

Verde: l’uso dell’IA è consentito.

La forza del modello non sta nella sua semplicità grafica, quanto nel fatto che rende esplicita la relazione tra tecnologia e obiettivo didattico. Se l’obiettivo di una verifica è accertare la capacità dello studente di produrre autonomamente un’argomentazione, l’IA potrebbe essere esclusa; se invece l’obiettivo è sviluppare la capacità di valutare criticamente una risposta prodotta da un sistema generativo, l’uso dell’IA diventa parte integrante dell’attività. Il colore, dunque, non dovrebbe essere associato allo strumento in sé, ma all’attività e all’obiettivo di apprendimento.

Non vuol dire quindi che “ChatGPT è rosso” oppure “ChatGPT è verde”. È l’insegnante a stabilire se, in quella specifica attività, l’IA costituisce un supporto, un oggetto di analisi oppure una scorciatoia che elimina il processo cognitivo che si intende valutare.

Questa prospettiva permetterebbe di superare una contrapposizione sterile tra sostenitori e oppositori dell’IA.

IA e apprendimento: quando la scorciatoia sostituisce il pensiero

Il problema pedagogico centrale è infatti il cognitive offloading[2], cioè la possibilità di delegare a una tecnologia una parte del lavoro cognitivo.

Se uno studente chiede a un chatbot di scrivere integralmente un testo, ottiene un prodotto, ma non necessariamente sviluppa le competenze necessarie per produrlo.

Se invece scrive il proprio testo, lo sottopone all’IA per ricevere un feedback, analizza le modifiche proposte e decide quali accettare, l’attività può diventare profondamente diversa.

È la strada sperimentata da Miriam Przybyla-Baum, insegnante di francese alla Cheshire Academy: gli studenti possono usare un modello linguistico per correggere i propri elaborati, devono poi analizzare le correzioni ricevute, chiedendosi quali sono corrette, quali no, e quali modificano inutilmente la loro voce. In questo caso l’IA non produce la risposta al posto dello studente, diventando oggetto di apprendimento, per cui lo studente esercita una competenza che diventerà sempre più importante, ovvero la capacità di giudicare criticamente l’output di una macchina.

Dall’AI detection all’AI literacy nella scuola

Questa esperienza suggerisce un cambio di prospettiva, per molto tempo infatti la domanda della scuola è stata come facciamo a capire se questo compito è stato scritto dall’IA oppure no? La domanda più utile e costruttiva potrebbe invece essere: come possiamo progettare un’attività nella quale lo studente debba dimostrare ciò che sa fare anche quando dispone dell’IA?”

Documentare il processo e verificare le fonti

Questo può significare chiedere allo studente di mettere in atto una serie di azioni, come per esempio

documentare le diverse fasi del lavoro;

confrontare la propria risposta con quella generata dall’IA;

individuare errori e informazioni non verificabili;

motivare le modifiche apportate;

verificare le fonti;

discutere oralmente il prodotto realizzato;

riflettere sul proprio processo di apprendimento.

La valutazione può quindi spostarsi progressivamente dal solo prodotto finale al rapporto tra processo, prodotto e capacità di riflessione.

L’IA a scuola come palestra di pensiero critico

C’è un ulteriore elemento che merita attenzione, considerando le riflessioni che la proposta operativa della Cheshire Academy propone.

Uno dei rischi più discussi dell’IA generativa è che gli studenti si abituino ad accettare come corretto ciò che una macchina produce con grande sicurezza, e allora proprio questa caratteristica può essere trasformata in una straordinaria opportunità didattica.

Trasformare errori e allucinazioni in materiale didattico

Un docente può fornire agli studenti una risposta generata dall’IA e porre diverse domande, per esempio: quali affermazioni devono essere verificate? Quali fonti possiamo utilizzare? Il linguaggio è appropriato?

In altre parole, l’errore dell’IA può diventare materiale didattico, la stessa allucinazione a sua volta non è soltanto un problema tecnico, può infatti diventare un’occasione per insegnare agli studenti a distinguere tra una risposta plausibile e una risposta affidabile.

È una competenza che va oltre l’uso di ChatGPT o altre IA generative e riguarda la più generale AI literacy: comprendere come funzionano questi sistemi, conoscerne i limiti, saper formulare richieste, verificare gli output e assumersi la responsabilità delle decisioni.

Il ruolo professionale del docente

Questo approccio comporta però una conseguenza importante per la professionalità docente. L’insegnante non può limitarsi a conoscere il funzionamento tecnico degli strumenti: deve essere in grado di fare una valutazione pedagogica del loro impiego.

L’IA può aiutare a generare idee, predisporre materiali, creare esercizi differenziati, produrre rubriche, riformulare testi, proporre esempi e offrire alternative, il risultato generato però non dovrebbe diventare automaticamente il prodotto finale.

Un principio particolarmente utile è quello sintetizzato nell’articolo di MIT Technology Review come “refine and replace”: generare, controllare, modificare, adattare. Il risultato finale è diverso dall’output dato dall’IA.

L’esperienza della Cheshire Academy suggerisce infine che il tema non può essere lasciato soltanto all’iniziativa del singolo docente.

Se ogni insegnante stabilisce autonomamente regole completamente diverse, lo studente può trovarsi davanti a una situazione incoerente: l’IA è vietata in una disciplina, ammessa senza limitazioni in un’altra, utilizzabile solo per la correzione in una terza. Da qui l’utilità di una AI classroom policy, costruita però non come semplice elenco di divieti, ma come strumento educativo.

Una scuola potrebbe definire alcuni principi comuni, creare una sorta di protocollo o vademecum: quando l’IA è vietata, quando è ammessa, quali strumenti possono essere utilizzati, come deve essere dichiarato il loro utilizzo, quali informazioni non devono essere inserite nei sistemi, come verificare le informazioni generate, quali competenze devono rimanere necessariamente in capo allo studente.

Il modello del semaforo quindi potrebbe diventare, in questo senso, un linguaggio comune dell’istituto.

Educare all’IA nella scuola italiana

La questione non è importare automaticamente il modello americano, il sistema scolastico italiano infatti ha caratteristiche proprie e richiede un’attenta riflessione sulle regole, sulla privacy, sulla protezione dei dati, sulla valutazione e sulla formazione del personale.

La lezione della Cheshire Academy può essere utile proprio perché sposta il problema: la scuola non deve necessariamente scegliere tra “IA sì” e “IA no”. La sfida non è costruire una scuola nella quale gli studenti non incontrino l’IA, dovrebbe e potrebbe essere invece quella di costruire una scuola nella quale, incontrandola, sappiano usarla senza smettere di pensare.

ChatGPT, per primo, e gli altri chatbot sono entrati non solo metaforicamente nelle tasche degli studenti attraverso gli smartphone, rendendo possibile ottenere in pochi secondi una spiegazione, un riassunto, una traduzione, un testo argomentativo o la soluzione di un esercizio.

La prima reazione della scuola – e quella del sistema educativo italiano non è stata da meno – è stata spesso quella del controllo: vietare, limitare, individuare l’uso dell’IA nei compiti, cercare strumenti capaci di riconoscere un testo generato artificialmente.

Questa strategia presenta un limite evidente: l’IA generativa è ormai parte dell’ambiente digitale nel quale gli studenti vivono e studiano. Pensare infatti di poterla semplicemente espellere dalla scuola rischia di produrre una contraddizione: vietarla nell’apprendimento significa lasciare che siano altri contesti, spesso privi di una guida educativa, a insegnare ai ragazzi come utilizzarla.

La questione diventa allora un’altra e sono in molti nel settore dell’istruzione a porsi la domanda, ovvero non come impedire l’uso dell’IA, piuttosto come educare a un suo uso intelligente.

La Cheshire Academy e l’educazione all’uso dell’IA a scuola

La scuola non impone né vieta agli insegnanti di utilizzare l’IA, e non prescrive un’unica piattaforma: chatbot generalisti come ChatGPT e Perplexity convivono con applicazioni pensate specificamente per la scuola, come MagicSchool. La formazione dei docenti si è concentrata sulle tecniche generali di utilizzo dell’IA — compreso il prompting — ma anche sui suoi limiti: errori, informazioni inventate, bias, problemi di affidabilità.

Il punto centrale, che vedremo emerge da questa esperienza nella scuola nordamericana, non è quindi quale tecnologia utilizzare, ma quali competenze sviluppare per utilizzarla. Conoscere un elenco di applicazioni conta meno che sviluppare una competenza trasferibile: sapere cosa chiedere all’IA, valutare ciò che restituisce, decidere se e come utilizzarlo. È una distinzione utile anche per la formazione dei docenti italiani.

Il modello del semaforo per l’IA nelle attività scolastiche

Uno degli strumenti più semplici sperimentati dalla Cheshire Academy è anche uno dei più interessanti dal punto di vista didattico è il traffic light model, il modello del semaforo, che come vedremo può essere facilmente esportabile come buona pratica.

Rosso, giallo e verde: le regole del modello

Le attività scolastiche vengono contrassegnate con tre colori.

Rosso: l’uso dell’IA non è consentito.

Giallo: l’uso dell’IA è consentito solo per alcune funzioni o attraverso determinati strumenti.

Verde: l’uso dell’IA è consentito.

La forza del modello non sta nella sua semplicità grafica, quanto nel fatto che rende esplicita la relazione tra tecnologia e obiettivo didattico. Se l’obiettivo di una verifica è accertare la capacità dello studente di produrre autonomamente un’argomentazione, l’IA potrebbe essere esclusa; se invece l’obiettivo è sviluppare la capacità di valutare criticamente una risposta prodotta da un sistema generativo, l’uso dell’IA diventa parte integrante dell’attività. Il colore, dunque, non dovrebbe essere associato allo strumento in sé, ma all’attività e all’obiettivo di apprendimento.

Non vuol dire quindi che “ChatGPT è rosso” oppure “ChatGPT è verde”. È l’insegnante a stabilire se, in quella specifica attività, l’IA costituisce un supporto, un oggetto di analisi oppure una scorciatoia che elimina il processo cognitivo che si intende valutare.

Questa prospettiva permetterebbe di superare una contrapposizione sterile tra sostenitori e oppositori dell’IA.

IA e apprendimento: quando la scorciatoia sostituisce il pensiero

Il problema pedagogico centrale è infatti il cognitive offloading[2], cioè la possibilità di delegare a una tecnologia una parte del lavoro cognitivo.

Se uno studente chiede a un chatbot di scrivere integralmente un testo, ottiene un prodotto, ma non necessariamente sviluppa le competenze necessarie per produrlo.

Se invece scrive il proprio testo, lo sottopone all’IA per ricevere un feedback, analizza le modifiche proposte e decide quali accettare, l’attività può diventare profondamente diversa.

È la strada sperimentata da Miriam Przybyla-Baum, insegnante di francese alla Cheshire Academy: gli studenti possono usare un modello linguistico per correggere i propri elaborati, devono poi analizzare le correzioni ricevute, chiedendosi quali sono corrette, quali no, e quali modificano inutilmente la loro voce. In questo caso l’IA non produce la risposta al posto dello studente, diventando oggetto di apprendimento, per cui lo studente esercita una competenza che diventerà sempre più importante, ovvero la capacità di giudicare criticamente l’output di una macchina.

La domanda più utile e costruttiva potrebbe invece essere: come possiamo progettare un’attività nella quale lo studente debba dimostrare ciò che sa fare anche quando dispone dell’IA?”

documentare le diverse fasi del lavoro;

confrontare la propria risposta con quella generata dall’IA;

individuare errori e informazioni non verificabili;

motivare le modifiche apportate;

verificare le fonti;

discutere oralmente il prodotto realizzato;

riflettere sul proprio processo di apprendimento.

La valutazione può quindi spostarsi progressivamente dal solo prodotto finale al rapporto tra processo, prodotto e capacità di riflessione.
